target: A national Election Day holiday would reduce work/school conflicts on Election Day enough to remove key scheduling barriers for voters.
objection: A federal holiday does not require private employers to close or give paid time off, so many private-sector, low-income, and hourly workers would still have to work and would not reliably gain the time off needed to vote.

target: Making Election Day a holiday would frame voting as a civic celebration and thereby increase turnout.
objection: Positive symbolism or civic framing cannot substitute for the practical ability to take time off to vote; if workers still lack time away from work, the celebratory framing will not overcome the barrier.

target: A national Election Day holiday is an effective strategy to increase voter turnout.
objection: Research indicates that making Election Day a holiday by itself is not an effective turnout strategy compared with other voting-access reforms.

target: The holiday will not help because some low-income workers would still face unavoidable work schedules.
objection: A reform does not need to eliminate every individual conflict to be useful; reducing scheduling barriers for many voters is enough to suppress barriers and increase participation relative to a normal workday.

target: A holiday only frames voting positively and therefore cannot help workers who lack time off.
objection: The civic framing is additive, not a substitute for access: a holiday can both strengthen motivation and reduce practical scheduling barriers at the same time.

target: A holiday-only approach is weak because other reforms could be enacted instead.
objection: Other access reforms such as employer time-off requirements and automatic registration can be implemented alongside a national Election Day holiday, so the holiday need not be a standalone measure.

target: Holiday framing and added motivation are enough to justify the policy.
objection: Civic motivation still cannot solve the core issue that voters need actual time away from work or school to cast a ballot.

target: A holiday would reliably increase turnout among the voters most affected by scheduling barriers.
objection: Because private employers are not required to provide time off for federal holidays, low-income and hourly workers would not reliably receive the practical paid time needed to vote.

target: Waiting time at polling places is not a meaningful barrier if a holiday helps staffing.
objection: Polling-place voting still takes time, including potential waiting; if a holiday increases poll-worker availability and reduces lines, it can reduce the time burden even without eliminating work entirely.

target: Reduced waiting time at polling places would solve the main problem for workers who must work.
objection: If a voter must still work, shorter lines do not create the necessary time away from the job, so reduced waiting time does not reliably overcome the primary barrier.

target: A national holiday would not reliably provide time off because federal law does not require private employers to close.
objection: In practice, federal holidays commonly change workplace and school schedules through closures, reduced operations, or accommodations, so a holiday would typically reduce scheduling conflicts for many people even if paid leave is not mandated.

target: The holiday will not help because the relevant voting hours remain the same.
objection: Even if polling hours do not formally change, reducing work/school conflicts on the day of the election still makes voting more feasible for millions of people.

target: A federal holiday would shift voting time windows outside work/school overlap.
objection: Polling hours are set by state law and administrative rules, not by federal holiday status, so a federal holiday does not automatically change the hours when voting is available.

target: Because not every individual conflict is eliminated, the holiday would not be worthwhile.
objection: A policy is worthwhile if it meaningfully reduces scheduling barriers for many voters, even if it does not eliminate every conflict for every person.

target: A federal holiday will likely give private-sector workers practical time off because of employment policies and flexibility.
objection: Many private-sector employees’ schedules are influenced by holiday pay, leave, union, or contract practices, so a federal holiday raises the practical likelihood of time off or schedule flexibility even without a legal mandate.

target: A federal holiday should be prioritized over more direct reforms.
objection: Research says a holiday by itself is not very effective, and prioritizing it could crowd out more reliable reforms such as employer time-off rules and automatic voter registration, especially harming low-income workers.

target: A federal holiday would not materially help because many low-income workers would still have to work.
objection: Many private-sector workers do receive schedule flexibility or time off from recognized federal holidays through employer practices, leave policies, union rules, or contracts, so a holiday can still reduce barriers in practice.

target: A federal holiday benefits low-income workers by giving them a work-free day.
objection: For many low-income and hourly workers, a federal holiday does not reliably provide wage-protected time off, and lost-wage costs can deter them from voting even if the day is formally a holiday.

target: The holiday will broadly improve participation across voters.
objection: Because many service, retail, and essential jobs must stay open, the holiday would produce uneven schedule relief and mainly help people whose workplaces can already close, leaving low-income workers with less benefit.

target: A holiday helps many people because they can vote early or by mail anyway.
objection: If many voters can already avoid Election Day conflicts by using early in-person or absentee/mail voting, then a holiday only affects the subset who would otherwise vote on Election Day and cannot switch to those options.

target: Early and absentee voting make an Election Day holiday unnecessary.
objection: Early and absentee options still require time during normal work hours for travel, requests, preparation, and deadlines, so they do not fully eliminate scheduling conflicts for many voters.

target: A holiday mainly changes the single election date and thus cannot solve weekday barriers.
objection: The holiday can still expand the practical ballot-handling time window for some administrative deadlines if those deadlines fall on the holiday and are adjusted to the next business day.

target: A federal holiday would reduce voting-hour overlap enough to matter.
objection: A federal holiday does not automatically expand polling hours or in-person voting availability, so the core scheduling constraint remains largely intact unless states separately change their rules.
